description: Microgravity solid-fuel combustion and fire safety investigation in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) aboard the ISS.

findings.observation: Gas-phase flame structure responds almost instantaneously to changes in forced airflow velocity, whereas thick solid fuels retain substantial heat long after flame size decreases.
findings.title: Flame responds instantly to airflow, thick solids keep their heat

findings.observation: At ultra-low airflow speeds (< 1 cm/s), flames transition to a dim, soot-free blue state that can persist for extended periods without extinguishing until airflow is completely stopped. A 15 mm PMMA sample persisted as a ~1 cm dim blue flame at low airflow and extinguished only after airflow was completely shut off to 0 cm/s.
findings.title: Dim blue flame persists at ultra-low airflow until ventilation stops

findings.observation: A localized nitrogen jet failed to extinguish a burning 15 mm PMMA sample because the thick solid fuel stored significant thermal energy; complete extinction required reducing forced airflow to 0 cm/s. Residual solid-phase heat can re-ignite vaporized fuel once the jet dissipates.
findings.title: Localised nitrogen jet can fail on preheated thick solids

findings.observation: Reducing oxygen concentration from 21% to 17% delays soot formation in PMMA combustion, keeping flames bluer and simplifying validation against numerical combustion models. At 17% O2 and 10-12 cm/s flow, a 2 cm PMMA sphere burns with a predominantly blue flame punctuated by occasional yellowish-red streaks as internal vapor bubbles burst through the flame.
findings.title: Lower oxygen delays soot formation in PMMA

name: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX)
research_category: Liquid Droplet Combustion and Flame Extinction
scientific_objective: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions.
transferability_note: Cool flames and low-temperature combustion can inform advanced combustion engines, improved fuel efficiency and reduced emissions; CO2, He and SF6 suppressant findings can lead to more efficient, less harmful suppression systems.

name: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE)
research_category: Gaseous Jet Diffusion Flames and Smoke Point
sample_geometry: Jet diffusion flames from co-flow burners
scientific_objective: The objective of SPICE is to better understand the complex process of combustion by observing flames in a microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and analogous ground experiments. Specific objectives: (1) Identify laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames under various co-flow conditions in microgravity. (2) Determine effects of burner diameter and co-flow velocity on luminous flame lengths and smoke points. (3) Quantify sooting propensity of different fuels, such as ethylene, propane, and propylene mixtures. (4) Validate correlation between luminous flame shape and residence time under microgravity. (5) Investigate impact of air and fuel flow rate variations on smoke point phenomena in space.
transferability_note: Could possibly provide insights to better fuel formulations and combustion processes.
